newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair wants next year's G7 to focus on jobs.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair wants next year's G7 to focus on jobs.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair, fresh from his first summit of the Group of Seven nations plus Russia, said on Tuesday he wants to concentrate on jobs and crime at next year's meeting in England.
Blair, who aides said was dismayed with the formalities at the Denver gathering, told Parliament he wants to return to the original idea for the summits.
Blair said he wanted the leaders of Russia and the world's main industrialised states to focus on "informal but substantive discussions" at the next summit in Birmingham, central England.

"This was my first G8 summit and I was struck by how much better the discussions were when we had time to focus on the key issues common to all our countries. Next year, I want to take that further and concentrate on fewer issues in greater depth...
"I want in particular to concentrate on two subjects: the issue of jobs and employability and the challenge posed by organised crime," Blair told parliament.

Aides say Blair wants the summit next year to be less of a "glorified photo call" and closer to the atmosphere of the informal "fireside chat" aimed for by French President Valery Giscard D'Estaing at the first economic summit in 1975.
Aides have raised the possibility of leaders heading off for at least half a day away from the prying eyes of the media.

Blair is hoping to make jobs and employability the centre of his foreign policy drives next year, when Britain will also hold the rotating European presidency, mirroring the focus of his new Labour government's domestic strategy.

"We all face the challenge of how to take advantage of increasing globalisation and provide new job opportunities. In many countries unemployment, particularly among young people, is far too high," Blair told parliament.
"We need to combine greater labour market flexibility with action to improve work incentives, skills and employability and reduce the risk of marginalisation."
